title: Unit 5: Torque and Rotational Dynamics

topics.name: Rotational inertia and Newton's second law for rotation
covers: Rotational dynamics and energy and Newton’s second law in rotational form

guide.title: Torque and rotational dynamics: review guide
guide.intro: Rotation has its own versions of force, mass, and acceleration: torque, rotational inertia, and angular acceleration. This unit covers objects in rotational equilibrium, the kinematics of turning, and Newton's second law for rotation.
guide.equationNote: g = 10 m/s² unless stated. Every rotational formula uses angles in radians.

sections.title: Torque and rotational equilibrium
body: Torque measures how effectively a force turns an object about an axis: τ = rF sin θ, where r is the distance from the axis to where the force acts and θ is the angle between r and F. Equivalently, τ = F × (lever arm).
An object in static equilibrium has zero net force and zero net torque about every axis. Choosing the axis at an unknown force removes that force from the torque equation.
points: Counterclockwise torques are usually taken as positive.
The weight of a uniform object acts at its center.
A force aimed straight through the axis produces no torque.

sections.title: Rotational kinematics
body: Angular position θ, angular velocity ω = dθ/dt, and angular acceleration α = dω/dt mirror the linear quantities. With constant α: ω = ω₀ + αt, θ = θ₀ + ω₀t + ½αt², and ω² = ω₀² + 2αΔθ.
A point at radius r on a rotating object moves at linear speed v = rω, with tangential acceleration a_t = rα and centripetal acceleration a_c = ω²r.
points: Every point on a rigid object has the same ω and α, but points farther from the axis move faster.
Use calculus when α changes with time.

sections.title: Rotational inertia and Newton's second law for rotation
body: Rotational inertia, I = Σmr² (or ∫r² dm), measures how hard it is to change an object's rotation. It depends on how the mass is spread around the axis. Common values: thin hoop MR², solid disk ½MR², solid sphere (2/5)MR², rod about its center (1/12)ML², rod about one end (1/3)ML².
Newton's second law for rotation is Στ = Iα. For a string wrapped around a pulley that has mass, the tensions on the two sides differ, and the pulley's rotational inertia reduces the acceleration.
points: Parallel-axis theorem: I = I_cm + Md², where d is the distance from the axis through the center of mass.
Rotational kinetic energy is ½Iω², and the work done by a torque is ∫τ dθ.
Mass far from the axis adds much more to I than mass near it.

example.prompt: A uniform rod of mass 1.2 kg and length 2.0 m can pivot freely about one end. It is held horizontal and released. Find its rotational inertia about the pivot and its angular acceleration just after release.
example.solution: I = (1/3)ML² = (1/3)(1.2)(2.0)² = 1.6 kg·m². The weight acts at the center, 1.0 m from the pivot, so τ = (1.2)(10)(1.0) = 12 N·m and α = τ/I = 12/1.6 = 7.5 rad/s².

misconceptions: “Torque depends only on the size of the force.”
It also depends on where the force acts and in which direction, relative to the axis.
It depends on how the mass is spread out around the axis.
“The tension is the same on both sides of a pulley that has mass.”
The difference in tension is what provides the torque that turns the pulley.
v = rω and the other rotational formulas need radians.

questions.prompt: A 20 N force is applied to the end of a wrench, 0.30 m from the bolt, at an angle of 30° to the wrench handle. What torque does it produce about the bolt?
questions.explanation: τ = rF sin θ = (0.30)(20)(sin 30°) = 6.0 × 0.50 = 3.0 N·m. Only the part of the force perpendicular to the handle turns the bolt.
choiceExplanations: 6.0 N·m would be the torque with the force perpendicular to the handle; at 30°, multiply by sin 30°.
5.2 N·m uses cos 30°; torque depends on the sine of the angle between r and F.
67 divides the force by the distance; torque multiplies them.

questions.prompt: A 30 kg child sits 2.0 m from the pivot of a seesaw. How far from the pivot, on the other side, must a 40 kg child sit to balance it? (Ignore the seesaw's own weight.)
questions.explanation: Balance the torques: (30)(g)(2.0) = (40)(g)d, so d = 60/40 = 1.5 m. The heavier child sits closer to the pivot.
choiceExplanations: 2.7 m puts the heavier child farther out, which would make that side's torque larger.
Equal distances balance only equal weights.
0.75 is the mass ratio 30/40, not a distance.

questions.prompt: A uniform 10 kg beam, 4.0 m long, rests on supports at its two ends. A 20 kg box sits 1.0 m from the left end. What upward force does the right support exert? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.explanation: Take torques about the left support: R(4.0) = (100 N)(2.0 m) + (200 N)(1.0 m) = 400 N·m, so R = 100 N. (The left support then provides 300 − 100 = 200 N.)
choiceExplanations: 200 N is the force from the left support, which is closer to the box.
150 N splits the total 300 N weight equally, but the box is not in the middle.
50 N leaves out the beam's own weight, which acts at its center.

questions.prompt: A wheel starts from rest and turns with a constant angular acceleration of 2.0 rad/s² for 5.0 s. Through what angle does it turn?
choiceExplanations: 50 rad leaves out the factor ½ in ½αt².
10 is the final angular velocity, αt, in rad/s.
5.0 is ½αt; the time must be squared.

questions.prompt: An object's angular position is θ(t) = 2t³ radians. What is its angular acceleration at t = 1.0 s?
questions.explanation: ω = dθ/dt = 6t² and α = dω/dt = 12t, so α(1.0) = 12 rad/s².
choiceExplanations: 6.0 is ω(1.0), the angular velocity in rad/s.
2.0 is θ(1.0), the angular position in radians.
18 adds ω and α together (6 + 12).

questions.prompt: A wheel of radius 0.40 m spins at 5.0 rad/s. How fast is a point on its rim moving?
choiceExplanations: 12.6 multiplies by 2π as well; ω is already in radians per second.
0.080 is r/ω; linear speed is r times ω.
5.0 is the angular speed; it must be multiplied by the radius.

questions.prompt: Two 2.0 kg masses are attached to the ends of a light rod 1.0 m long. What is the rotational inertia about an axis through the middle of the rod, perpendicular to it?
questions.explanation: Each mass is 0.50 m from the axis: I = Σmr² = 2 × (2.0)(0.50)² = 1.0 kg·m².
choiceExplanations: 4.0 uses the full length, 1.0 m, as each mass's distance from the axis.
2.0 uses mr instead of mr²; the distance must be squared.
0.50 counts only one of the two masses.

questions.prompt: A solid disk (I = ½MR²) of mass 4.0 kg and radius 0.50 m spins about its axis. A net torque of 2.0 N·m acts on it. What is its angular acceleration?
choiceExplanations: 1.0 multiplies τ by I; α = τ/I.
2.0 rad/s² uses I = MR², the hoop's value, instead of ½MR².
0.25 is I/τ, the ratio upside down.

questions.prompt: A 2.0 kg block hangs from a light string wrapped around a pulley that is a uniform solid disk of mass 4.0 kg, free to turn on a frictionless axle. What is the block's acceleration? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.explanation: Block: mg − T = ma. Pulley: TR = (½MR²)(a/R), so T = ½Ma. Adding: mg = (m + ½M)a, so a = 20/(2.0 + 2.0) = 5.0 m/s².
choiceExplanations: 10 m/s² ignores the pulley; the string tension slows the block.
3.3 m/s² uses I = MR², which is for a hoop, not a solid disk.
6.7 m/s² uses I = ¼MR², which is a disk's inertia about a diameter, not about its axle.
